description: The commands that change geometry that already exists: moving, copying, arraying and aligning objects, trimming and extending them against each other, editing polylines, splines, hatches, text, attributes and blocks, and repairing or cleaning up a drawing. Every one can be typed at the command prompt, put in a script or macro, or called from AutoLISP with (command "_MOVE" ...); several have a leading-hyphen variant that suppresses the dialog so scripts can drive them.

tools.name: ERASE
tools.description: Delete the selected objects from the drawing. It is the most-used modify command and the one most often driven from a selection set in LISP, because any ssget filter can be handed straight to it. Nothing is asked after the selection is complete, so it is safe in scripts as long as the selection is deterministic.
tools.usage:
ERASE  (alias E; also the Delete key when PICKFIRST is 1)
Select objects: <selection> | ALL | L | P | W | C | F | CP | WP | R | A
Select objects: Enter

parameters.name: ALL
parameters.description: Select every object in the drawing except those on frozen or locked layers.

parameters.name: Window (W) / Crossing (C)
parameters.description: Window selects only objects wholly inside the box; Crossing also takes anything the box touches.

parameters.name: Fence (F)
parameters.description: Select every object crossed by a multi-segment fence line - the quickest way to pick a row of similar items.

parameters.name: Last (L) / Previous (P)
parameters.description: The most recently created object, or the previous selection set. P is how a script re-uses the selection made by a preceding SELECT command.

parameters.name: Remove (R) / Add (A)
parameters.description: Switch between taking objects out of and putting them back into the current selection set.

parameters.name: PICKFIRST
parameters.description: System variable enabling noun-verb editing: when 1, objects selected before the command is started are used automatically and the Select objects prompt is skipped.

tools.example:
; Erase everything on a scratch layer
SELECT
ALL

ERASE
P


; AutoLISP: erase all text on layer NOTES-OLD
(setq ss (ssget "_X" '((0 . "TEXT,MTEXT") (8 . "NOTES-OLD"))))
(if ss (command "_ERASE" ss ""))
tools.notes: OOPS restores the objects from the last ERASE without undoing anything done since; U or UNDO rolls the whole operation back. Objects on locked or frozen layers cannot be erased, which is the usual reason an ALL selection deletes fewer objects than expected. PICKADD 0 makes each new pick replace the selection instead of adding to it and is a common source of confusion.

tools.name: OOPS
tools.description: Restore the objects removed by the most recent ERASE, without undoing any work done since. It also brings back the source objects consumed by BLOCK or WBLOCK when the Delete option was used, which is its other classic use. Only the last erased set is remembered, and only one level deep.
tools.usage:
OOPS
(no prompts - the last erased selection set is restored in place)

parameters.name: last erased set
parameters.description: The selection set of the most recent ERASE in this session; earlier erasures are not recoverable with OOPS.

parameters.name: after BLOCK / WBLOCK
parameters.description: Restores geometry that was deleted when it was converted into a block definition or written out to a file.

parameters.name: no arguments
parameters.description: The command takes no options and asks nothing, so it is safe to put in a script or a menu macro immediately after an ERASE or a -BLOCK.

tools.example:
; Make a block from the geometry, deleting the originals,
; then put the originals back without losing the new block
-BLOCK
VALVE_GATE
0,0
ALL

OOPS

; Accidental deletion mid-script
ERASE
ALL

OOPS
tools.notes: OOPS is not UNDO: it only puts erased objects back and leaves every later command intact, which is exactly why it is preferred after BLOCK. It cannot restore objects deleted by PURGE, by exploding, or by a command that consumed them such as JOIN or REGION - use UNDO for those.

tools.name: MOVE
tools.description: Move the selected objects by a displacement given as two points or as a single vector. It is the workhorse of layout changes and the command most often scripted, because the base point and second point can both be typed as absolute or relative coordinates. Use it with object snaps to reposition a part exactly onto a feature of another.
tools.usage:
MOVE  (alias M)
Select objects: <selection>
Select objects: Enter
Specify base point or [Displacement] <Displacement>: <point> | D
Specify second point or <use first point as displacement>: <point> | Enter

parameters.name: base point
parameters.description: Reference point on the objects being moved; any object snap can be used to make it exact.

parameters.name: second point
parameters.description: Destination of the base point. Type @dx,dy for a relative move or @dist<angle for a polar move.

parameters.name: Displacement (D)
parameters.description: Give a single vector from the origin instead of two points; pressing Enter at the second prompt treats the first point the same way.

parameters.name: ORTHOMODE / OSMODE
parameters.description: System variables for orthogonal constraint and running object snaps, which decide how interactive moves land.

tools.example:
; Move a selection 250 units to the right and 100 up
MOVE
ALL

0,0
@250,100

; AutoLISP: nudge every block named TAG onto the origin of its layer grid
(setq ss (ssget "_X" '((0 . "INSERT") (2 . "TAG"))))
(command "_MOVE" ss "" '(0 0 0) '(0 5 0))
tools.notes: MOVE with the Displacement option is the safest form in scripts because it needs only one coordinate. To move objects between layouts or drawings use the clipboard commands COPYBASE and PASTEORIG, which preserve coordinates. Grips give the same result interactively: select an object, click a grip and the default grip mode is stretch, with MOVE on the grip menu.

tools.name: COPY
tools.description: Duplicate the selected objects at a new location. Since AutoCAD 2006 the command repeats automatically so several copies can be placed in one run, and the Array option produces a quick linear row of copies without going to the ARRAY command. The mOde option switches between single and multiple behaviour for the rest of the session.
tools.usage:
COPY  (alias CO or CP)
Select objects: <selection>
Specify base point or [Displacement/mOde] <Displacement>: <point> | D | O
Specify second point or [Array] <use first point as displacement>: <point> | A
Specify second point or [Array/Exit/Undo] <Exit>: <point> | A | E | U

parameters.name: mOde (O)
parameters.description: Single or Multiple. Single ends after one copy; Multiple keeps repeating until Enter.

parameters.name: COPYMODE
parameters.description: System variable holding the same setting: 0 lets the command repeat, 1 makes it stop after one copy.

parameters.name: Array (A)
parameters.description: Place a number of copies in a line; you then give the item count and either the spacing of the second item or Fit to spread them between two points.

parameters.name: Displacement (D)
parameters.description: Give the offset as one vector instead of two points.

parameters.name: Undo (U)
parameters.description: Remove the last copy placed without leaving the command.

tools.example:
; Four copies of a hole, 50 apart
COPY
L

0,0
@50,0
@100,0
@150,0
@200,0


; Same thing with the Array option
COPY
L

0,0
A
5
@50,0

; AutoLISP form
(command "_COPY" (ssget "_P") "" '(0 0) '(50 0))
tools.notes: For regular patterns ARRAYRECT and ARRAYPOLAR are better because the result stays associative and the count can be changed later. COPYBASE (Ctrl+Shift+C) and PASTECLIP move objects between drawings with a chosen base point; PASTEORIG pastes at the original coordinates.

tools.name: ROTATE
tools.description: Rotate the selected objects about a base point by an absolute angle, or by a Reference angle measured from existing geometry. The Copy option leaves the originals in place and rotates a duplicate, which is how radial details are built up by hand. Positive angles follow ANGDIR, which is counter-clockwise by default.
tools.usage:
ROTATE  (alias RO)
Current positive angle in UCS:  ANGDIR=counterclockwise  ANGBASE=0
Select objects: <selection>
Specify base point: <point>
Specify rotation angle or [Copy/Reference] <0>: <angle> | C | R

parameters.name: base point
parameters.description: The pivot. Objects rotate about this point, so pick a centre, corner or insertion point deliberately.

parameters.name: Copy (C)
parameters.description: Keep the original objects and rotate a copy.

parameters.name: Reference (R)
parameters.description: Give a current reference angle (or two points on existing geometry) and then the angle it should become - the way to straighten something skewed by an unknown amount.

parameters.name: ANGDIR
parameters.description: System variable for the positive direction: 0 counter-clockwise (default), 1 clockwise.

parameters.name: ANGBASE
parameters.description: System variable for the direction of angle zero in the current UCS.

tools.example:
; Rotate a part 30 degrees about its insertion point
ROTATE
L

0,0
30

; Straighten a skewed detail using Reference
ROTATE
ALL

100,100
R
100,100
180,140
0

; Rotate a copy
(command "_ROTATE" (ssget "_P") "" '(0 0) "_C" 90)
tools.notes: Reference with two picked points is the reliable way to align to geometry whose angle you do not know. Blocks rotate about the base point given here, not their own insertion point, so the two must be the same if the insertion point must not move. ALIGN does rotation and translation (and optional scaling) in one step when both source and destination points are known.

tools.name: SCALE
tools.description: Enlarge or reduce the selected objects uniformly about a base point. The scale factor can be typed directly, or derived with the Reference option by stating a known current length and the length it should become - the standard way to rescale an imported drawing or a scanned image to a known dimension. Scaling is always uniform in X, Y and Z.
tools.usage:
SCALE  (alias SC)
Select objects: <selection>
Specify base point: <point>
Specify scale factor or [Copy/Reference] <1.0000>: <factor> | C | R
(Reference) Specify reference length <1>: / Specify new length or [Points]:

parameters.name: scale factor
parameters.description: Multiplier greater than 1 enlarges, between 0 and 1 reduces. Negative factors are not accepted; use MIRROR instead.

parameters.name: base point
parameters.description: The point that stays fixed. Everything else moves away from or towards it.

parameters.name: Copy (C)
parameters.description: Leave the originals and scale a duplicate.

parameters.name: Reference (R)
parameters.description: Enter the current length of a known feature then the required length; Points lets you pick the two ends of the reference instead of typing it.

tools.example:
; Convert a drawing from inches to millimetres
SCALE
ALL

0,0
25.4

; Rescale a traced image so a known wall is 5000 long
SCALE
L

0,0
R
P
(pick one end)
(pick the other end)
5000
tools.notes: SCALE changes real geometry. To change only the displayed size of text or of annotative objects use SCALETEXT or the annotation scale, not SCALE. Dimensions scaled with their geometry keep measuring correctly because the measurement is associative, but their text height follows DIMSCALE or the annotative scale, not this command.

tools.name: STRETCH
tools.description: Move the endpoints that fall inside a crossing selection while leaving the rest of each object anchored, which lengthens or reshapes geometry instead of relocating it. It is the correct way to make a room bigger, move a wall, or shift a row of holes while keeping everything connected. Objects wholly inside the crossing window are simply moved.
tools.usage:
STRETCH  (alias S)
Select objects to stretch by crossing-window or crossing-polygon...
Select objects: C <first corner> <opposite corner> | CP <points>
Select objects: Enter
Specify base point or [Displacement] <Displacement>: <point> | D
Specify second point or <use first point as displacement>: <point>

parameters.name: Crossing (C)
parameters.description: The only selection mode that produces stretching; a Window selection or individual picks make STRETCH behave exactly like MOVE.

parameters.name: CPolygon (CP)
parameters.description: Crossing polygon, for picking an irregular region of endpoints.

parameters.name: base point / second point
parameters.description: The displacement applied to every selected endpoint. Type @dx,dy for an exact amount.

parameters.name: Displacement (D)
parameters.description: Give the offset as a single vector.

parameters.name: crossed vs enclosed
parameters.description: Endpoints inside the crossing region move; endpoints outside stay put. Circles, text, blocks and other point-defined objects move only if their defining point is inside.

tools.example:
; Push the right-hand wall of a room 500 further right
STRETCH
C
4800,-500
6000,4500

0,0
@500,0

; AutoLISP: stretch using an explicit crossing window
(command "_STRETCH" "_C" '(4800 -500) '(6000 4500) "" '(0 0) '(500 0))
tools.notes: Only the most recent crossing selection is used for the stretch, so building a selection from several windows does not work as expected. Dimensions whose definition points are caught in the window update their measurement automatically, which is the main reason to stretch rather than move and re-dimension. Hatches lose or keep their fit depending on whether they are associative.

tools.name: LENGTHEN
tools.description: Change the length of an open object or the included angle of an arc without needing a boundary to trim or extend to. Selecting an object with no option first reports its current length, which makes it a quick measuring tool. It works on lines, arcs, elliptical arcs, open polylines and open splines, but not on closed objects.
tools.usage:
LENGTHEN  (alias LEN)
Select an object to measure or [DElta/Percent/Total/DYnamic] <Total>: <object> | DE | P | T | DY
(DElta) Enter delta length or [Angle] <0>:
(Percent) Enter percentage length <100>:
(Total) Specify total length or [Angle] <1.0>:
Select an object to change or [Undo]:

parameters.name: DElta (DE)
parameters.description: Add or subtract a length increment; a negative value shortens. The Angle suboption changes an arc's included angle by an increment.

parameters.name: Percent (P)
parameters.description: Set the new length as a percentage of the current one; 50 halves it, 200 doubles it.

parameters.name: Total (T)
parameters.description: Set the absolute overall length, or with Angle the absolute included angle of an arc.

parameters.name: DYnamic (DY)
parameters.description: Drag the nearest endpoint; the other end stays fixed.

parameters.name: pick end
parameters.description: The end you click nearest to is the one that changes, for every option.

tools.example:
; Extend every centre line by 5 at each end
LENGTHEN
DE
5
(pick near one end)
(pick near the other end)


; Set an arc to exactly 90 degrees
LENGTHEN
T
A
90
(pick the arc)
tools.notes: LENGTHEN cannot shorten an object past zero and does nothing to closed polylines, circles or ellipses. When a boundary exists, TRIM and EXTEND are usually faster; LENGTHEN is for when there is nothing to trim against. Selecting an object at the first prompt with no option chosen simply reports its length, which is often quicker than DIST.

tools.name: TRIM
tools.description: Cut objects back at their intersections with other objects. From AutoCAD 2021 the command runs in Quick mode by default: every visible object acts as a cutting edge, so you just pick the pieces to remove, and holding Shift while picking extends instead of trimming. Standard mode, where cutting edges are selected first, is still available through the mOde option for drawings and scripts that depend on it.
tools.usage:
TRIM  (alias TR)
Current settings: Mode = Quick
Select object to trim or shift-select to extend or
[cuTting edges/Crossing/mOde/Project/eRase]:

; Standard mode
Current settings: Projection=UCS, Edge=None, Mode=Standard
Select cutting edges ...
Select objects or <select all>: Enter
Select object to trim or shift-select to extend or
[Fence/Crossing/mOde/Project/Edge/eRase/Undo]:

parameters.name: mOde (O)
parameters.description: Switch between Quick (all objects are cutting edges, the 2021 and later default) and Standard (cutting edges are selected first).

parameters.name: TRIMEXTENDMODE
parameters.description: System variable that stores which of those two modes TRIM and EXTEND start in, so an office standard or a script can force the legacy behaviour.

parameters.name: shift-select
parameters.description: Holding Shift while picking switches the command to extending - the same key works the other way round inside EXTEND.

parameters.name: cuTting edges (T)
parameters.description: In Quick mode, select a specific set of edges instead of using everything.

parameters.name: Crossing (C) / Fence (F)
parameters.description: Free-form drag selections for picking many pieces at once; a fence line trims everything it crosses.

parameters.name: Edge (E) / EDGEMODE
parameters.description: Standard mode only: Extend makes a cutting edge act as if it were infinitely long so it can trim objects it does not actually reach; No extend requires a real intersection. EDGEMODE holds the setting.

parameters.name: Project (P) / PROJMODE
parameters.description: How intersections are found in 3D: None (true 3D), Ucs (project onto the XY plane of the current UCS) or View (project onto the view plane).

parameters.name: eRase (R)
parameters.description: Delete a whole object without leaving the command, for the stray leftovers trimming produces.

tools.example:
; 2021 and later - Quick mode, pick the pieces to remove
TRIM
(pick a segment)
(pick another segment)


; Force legacy behaviour in a script that predates 2021
TRIMEXTENDMODE 0
TRIM
(select cutting edges)

(select objects to trim)


; AutoLISP: trim everything crossing a fence, using all edges
(command "_TRIM" "" "_F" '(0 50) '(500 50) "" "")
tools.notes: Hatches, text and blocks cannot be trimmed; only their boundaries can. In Quick mode a stray object far away can still act as an edge, so zoom to the work area or use cuTting edges when the result looks wrong. Shift-select is the single most useful habit in both TRIM and EXTEND because it removes the need to swap commands. BREAK is the alternative when there is no cutting edge at all.

tools.name: EXTEND
tools.description: Lengthen objects until they meet a boundary edge. It is the mirror image of TRIM and shares its settings: from AutoCAD 2021 it runs in Quick mode where every visible object is a potential boundary, and holding Shift while picking trims instead of extending. Objects extend in the direction of the end you pick nearest to.
tools.usage:
EXTEND  (alias EX)
Current settings: Mode = Quick
Select object to extend or shift-select to trim or
[Boundary edges/Crossing/mOde/Project]:

; Standard mode
Select boundary edges ...
Select objects or <select all>: Enter
Select object to extend or shift-select to trim or
[Fence/Crossing/mOde/Project/Edge/Undo]:

parameters.name: mOde (O)
parameters.description: Quick or Standard, shared with TRIM and stored in TRIMEXTENDMODE.

parameters.name: Boundary edges (B)
parameters.description: In Quick mode, restrict extension to a chosen set of boundaries instead of everything visible.

parameters.name: shift-select
parameters.description: Holding Shift trims the picked object instead of extending it.

parameters.name: Edge (E) / EDGEMODE
parameters.description: Extend mode lets an object reach the implied, infinite extension of a boundary; No extend requires the boundary to actually cross the object's path.

parameters.name: Project (P) / PROJMODE
parameters.description: None, Ucs or View - how the intersection is computed for objects that are not coplanar.

parameters.name: pick end
parameters.description: The end nearest the pick point is the one that grows; picking the wrong half is the usual reason nothing happens.

tools.example:
; Extend two lines up to a wall face
EXTEND
(pick near the right end of the first line)
(pick near the right end of the second)


; Extend to an implied intersection in Standard mode
TRIMEXTENDMODE 0
EXTEND
(select the boundary)

E
E
(pick the object to extend)


; Extend everything crossed by a fence
(command "_EXTEND" "" "_F" '(0 0) '(0 3000) "" "")
tools.notes: Nothing happens when the object, if extended, would never reach the boundary - switch Edge to Extend so the boundary is treated as infinite. A closed polyline cannot be extended. LENGTHEN is the command to use when there is no boundary to extend to.

tools.name: BREAK
tools.description: Remove the part of an object between two picked points, or split it into two objects at a single point. It is how a line is opened up for a symbol to sit in, and how a construction line or ray is turned into finite geometry. Breaking a circle removes the arc running counter-clockwise from the first point to the second.
tools.usage:
BREAK  (alias BR)
Select object: <object - the pick point is also the first break point>
Specify second break point or [First point]: <point> | F | @
(First) Specify first break point: / Specify second break point:

BREAKATPOINT  (AutoCAD 2021 and later)
Select object: / Specify break point:

parameters.name: First point (F)
parameters.description: Re-specify the first break point, which is needed whenever the point used to select the object is not where the break should start.

parameters.name: @ as second point
parameters.description: Splits the object in two at the first break point with no gap - the classic keyboard trick, now also available as BREAKATPOINT.

parameters.name: direction on arcs and circles
parameters.description: The removed piece always runs counter-clockwise from the first to the second point, so swapping the picks keeps the other half.

parameters.name: points off the object
parameters.description: A break point picked away from the object is projected onto its nearest point, which is convenient but can surprise you at corners.

tools.example:
; Open a 20 wide gap in a line for a symbol
BREAK
(select the line)
F
490,0
510,0

; Split a polyline in two without a gap
BREAK
(select the polyline)
F
(pick the split point)
@

; Same thing in 2021 and later
BREAKATPOINT
(select the object)
(pick the split point)
tools.notes: A closed polyline or circle becomes an open arc or polyline; a circle cannot be broken into two pieces in one operation. BREAK cannot split a block, text or hatch. Use object snaps for the break points, and remember the object-selection pick doubles as the first break point unless you use First. JOIN reverses the operation when the pieces are still collinear or concentric.

tools.name: JOIN
tools.description: Combine separate collinear or contiguous objects into one. Lines that lie on the same infinite line, arcs on the same imaginary circle, polylines that share endpoints, and splines, elliptical arcs and helixes that meet can all be merged. It is the standard repair after trimming, breaking or exploding, and the way to turn a chain of lines and arcs into a single polyline that can be offset or measured.
tools.usage:
JOIN  (alias J)
Select source object or multiple objects to join at once: <selection>
Select objects to join: Enter
(for arcs and elliptical arcs) [cLose]: L closes the arc into a full circle or ellipse

parameters.name: collinear lines
parameters.description: Lines must lie on the same infinite line; gaps between them are allowed and are closed by the join.

parameters.name: arcs
parameters.description: Arcs must lie on the same imaginary circle. They are joined counter-clockwise from the source arc, so the result can sweep the long way round.

parameters.name: cLose (L)
parameters.description: Turn the selected arc into a circle, or an elliptical arc into a full ellipse, instead of joining.

parameters.name: result type
parameters.description: Joining a mixture of lines and arcs that meet end to end produces a polyline; joining collinear lines produces a single line.

parameters.name: coplanar requirement
parameters.description: All objects must be in the same plane; objects at different elevations will not join.

tools.example:
; Rebuild a profile that was exploded into lines and arcs
JOIN
ALL


; Turn an arc back into a full circle
JOIN
(select the arc)
L

; AutoLISP: join every line on a layer
(setq ss (ssget "_X" '((0 . "LINE") (8 . "PROFILE"))))
(command "_JOIN" ss "")
tools.notes: If the objects do not join, the usual causes are a difference in elevation, a slight angular mismatch, or arcs that are not truly concentric - check with the Properties palette. PEDIT with the Join option and a fuzz distance is the tolerant alternative: it will bridge small gaps that JOIN refuses. OVERKILL is the right tool when the problem is duplicates rather than fragments.

tools.name: CHAMFER
tools.description: Bevel the corner between two lines, either by two distances or by a distance and an angle. Settings are sticky, so the same bevel can be applied around a part without retyping, and the Polyline option chamfers every vertex of a polyline at once. Holding Shift while selecting the second object forces a zero chamfer, which is the quickest way to close a corner to a sharp point.
tools.usage:
CHAMFER  (alias CHA)
(TRIM mode) Current chamfer Dist1 = 0.0000, Dist2 = 0.0000
Select first line or [Undo/Polyline/Distance/Angle/Trim/mEthod/Multiple]:
Select second line or shift-select to apply corner or [Distance/Angle/Method]:

parameters.name: Distance (D)
parameters.description: Set the first and second chamfer distances, measured back along each object from the intersection.

parameters.name: Angle (A)
parameters.description: Set a distance along the first line plus the angle of the chamfer from that line.

parameters.name: mEthod (E)
parameters.description: Choose whether the command uses the two distances or the distance-and-angle pair; held in CHAMMODE.

parameters.name: Polyline (P)
parameters.description: Apply the current chamfer to every vertex of a 2D polyline in one operation.

parameters.name: Trim (T) / TRIMMODE
parameters.description: Trim cuts the original lines back to the chamfer, No trim leaves them full length. TRIMMODE 0 turns trimming off for both CHAMFER and FILLET.

parameters.name: Multiple (M)
parameters.description: Keep chamfering pairs of objects until Enter, instead of ending after one.

parameters.name: CHAMFERA / CHAMFERB / CHAMFERC / CHAMFERD
parameters.description: System variables holding the two distances, and the distance and angle used by the angle method.

parameters.name: shift-select
parameters.description: Applies a zero-distance chamfer, extending or trimming both objects to a sharp corner.

tools.example:
; 2 x 2 chamfer on every corner of a rectangle
CHAMFER
D
2
2
P
(select the polyline)

; Distance-and-angle chamfer, repeated
CHAMFER
E
A
A
3
30
M
(select first line) (select second line)
(select first line) (select second line)


; AutoLISP: 1 mm break edge between two lines
(command "_CHAMFER" "_D" 1.0 1.0 pt1 pt2)
tools.notes: The two objects do not have to touch: CHAMFER extends or trims them to the implied corner. Chamfer distances stay set until changed, so reset them to 0 before drawing a square corner, or use shift-select. CHAMFEREDGE is the separate command for 3D solids; RECTANG can apply a chamfer as the rectangle is drawn.

tools.name: FILLET
tools.description: Round the corner between two objects with an arc of a given radius, extending or trimming them as needed. A radius of 0 produces a sharp corner instead, which is the standard way to close a gap between two lines that should meet, and holding Shift while picking the second object forces that behaviour without changing the stored radius. The Polyline option rounds every vertex of a polyline in one pass.
tools.usage:
FILLET  (alias F)
Current settings: Mode = TRIM, Radius = 0.0000
Select first object or [Undo/Polyline/Radius/Trim/Multiple]:
Select second object or shift-select to apply corner or [Radius]:

parameters.name: Radius (R)
parameters.description: Fillet radius; stored in FILLETRAD and reused until changed. 0 makes a sharp corner.

parameters.name: Polyline (P)
parameters.description: Fillet every vertex of a 2D polyline at once; vertices too short for the radius are left alone.

parameters.name: Trim (T) / TRIMMODE
parameters.description: Trim cuts the originals back to the arc, No trim leaves them intact and just adds the arc.

parameters.name: Multiple (M)
parameters.description: Keep filleting pairs of objects until Enter.

parameters.name: shift-select
parameters.description: Temporarily applies radius 0 to make a sharp corner, leaving FILLETRAD unchanged.

parameters.name: parallel lines
parameters.description: Filleting two parallel lines draws a semicircular end cap between them; the radius setting is ignored.

tools.example:
; 5 mm radius on all corners of a polyline
FILLET
R
5
P
(select the polyline)

; Close a corner between two lines that do not meet
FILLET
R
0
(select the first line)
(select the second line)

; AutoLISP: fillet without trimming
(command "_FILLET" "_T" "_N" "_R" 10.0 pt1 pt2)
tools.notes: FILLET works on lines, polylines, arcs, circles, ellipses, splines, rays and construction lines, and on two parallel lines. BLEND (also reached as BLENDCURVE) is the related command that joins two open curves with a tangent or smooth spline instead of an arc and leaves both curves untouched; it is not given its own entry in this catalog. FILLETEDGE is the 3D solid equivalent, and RECTANG can fillet corners as the rectangle is drawn.

tools.name: EXPLODE
tools.description: Break a compound object into its component parts: a block into the objects it contains, a polyline into lines and arcs, a dimension or leader into lines, arrowheads and text, an mtext into single-line text, a hatch into individual pattern lines, an associative array into independent copies. Use it when something must be edited piece by piece, and be aware that information is lost in the process.
tools.usage:
EXPLODE  (alias X)
Select objects: <selection>
Select objects: Enter

parameters.name: blocks
parameters.description: One level per pass: a block containing blocks needs exploding again. Attribute values are lost and revert to attribute definitions.

parameters.name: polylines
parameters.description: Width and tangent information is discarded; the result is plain lines and arcs on the polyline's layer.

parameters.name: dimensions and leaders
parameters.description: Become lines, 2D solids and text, losing associativity to the geometry they measured.

parameters.name: hatches
parameters.description: Become hundreds or thousands of separate line objects; almost always the wrong thing to do to a hatch.

parameters.name: associative arrays
parameters.description: Exploding destroys the association, after which ARRAYEDIT can no longer change the count or spacing.

parameters.name: EXPLMODE
parameters.description: System variable controlling whether blocks with unequal X, Y and Z scale factors can be exploded.

tools.example:
; Explode every block named DETAIL_TAG
(setq ss (ssget "_X" '((0 . "INSERT") (2 . "DETAIL_TAG"))))
(command "_EXPLODE" ss)

; Explode a nested block completely
EXPLODE
L

EXPLODE
ALL
tools.notes: A block defined with 'Allow exploding' cleared cannot be exploded at all. XPLODE is the version that lets you set the layer, colour, linetype and lineweight of the resulting objects instead of accepting the defaults. Exploding blocks wholesale is the most common cause of bloated, unmanageable drawings - prefer BEDIT or REFEDIT to change the definition instead.

tools.name: XPLODE
tools.description: Explode compound objects while controlling the properties the pieces end up with. Ordinary EXPLODE sends block contents back to whatever layer, colour and linetype they were drawn on; XPLODE can instead force them onto a chosen layer, give them an explicit colour or linetype, or make them inherit the properties of the block reference they came from. Use it when exploding must not scatter geometry across unwanted layers.
tools.usage:
XPLODE
Select objects: <selection>
Enter an option [Individually/Globally] <Globally>: I | G
Enter an option [All/Color/LAyer/LType/LWeight/Inherit from parent block/Explode] <Explode>:

parameters.name: Individually / Globally
parameters.description: Apply the settings to each selected object in turn, or the same settings to all of them at once.

parameters.name: All (A)
parameters.description: Prompt for colour, linetype, lineweight and layer in sequence.

parameters.name: LAyer (LA)
parameters.description: Put every resulting object on a named layer, regardless of where it was drawn.

parameters.name: Color (C) / LType (LT) / LWeight (LW)
parameters.description: Assign an explicit colour, linetype or lineweight to the results, or BYLAYER / BYBLOCK.

parameters.name: Inherit from parent block (I)
parameters.description: Give the pieces the properties the block reference had. This only works for geometry drawn on layer 0 with colour, linetype and lineweight set to BYBLOCK.

parameters.name: Explode (E)
parameters.description: Behave exactly like EXPLODE, accepting the components' own properties.

tools.example:
; Explode tags and force everything onto the ANNO layer
XPLODE
(select the blocks)

G
LA
ANNO

; Explode so the pieces keep the look they had inside the block

L

G
I
tools.notes: Inherit from parent block silently falls back to the objects' own properties when they were not drawn on layer 0 with BYBLOCK properties, which is the usual reason the result looks wrong. XPLODE cannot explode objects that EXPLODE cannot explode either, such as blocks flagged as non-explodable or xrefs.

tools.name: OFFSET
tools.description: Create a parallel copy of an object at a given distance or through a picked point. It is the backbone of 2D drafting: wall faces, pipe runs, setbacks, machining allowances and concentric profiles are all built by offsetting. The command repeats so one distance can be applied to many objects, and the Erase and Layer options control what happens to the source and where the copy lands.
tools.usage:
OFFSET  (alias O)
Current settings: Erase source=No  Layer=Source  OFFSETGAPTYPE=0
Specify offset distance or [Through/Erase/Layer] <1.0000>: <dist> | T | E | L
Select object to offset or [Exit/Undo] <Exit>: <object>
Specify point on side to offset or [Exit/Multiple/Undo] <Exit>: <point> | M | E | U

parameters.name: Through (T)
parameters.description: Offset through a picked point instead of by a typed distance - the way to offset to an existing intersection or node.

parameters.name: Erase (E)
parameters.description: Delete the source object after offsetting, turning the command into a parallel move.

parameters.name: Layer (L)
parameters.description: Put the new object on the Source object's layer or on the Current layer. Setting this to Current is what keeps offset setting-out lines off the wall layer.

parameters.name: Multiple (M)
parameters.description: Keep offsetting the same object repeatedly at the same distance, each copy taken from the previous one.

parameters.name: OFFSETDIST
parameters.description: System variable holding the last distance used; a negative value means the Through option is current.

parameters.name: OFFSETGAPTYPE
parameters.description: How gaps are closed when offsetting a polyline outwards: 0 extends the segments to meet, 1 fills the gap with a fillet arc, 2 fills it with a chamfer.

tools.example:
; Wall faces 100 either side of a centre line
OFFSET
100
(select the centre line)
(pick above)
(select the centre line)
(pick below)


; Five parallel lines 25 apart, on the current layer
OFFSET
L
C

25
(select the line)
M
(pick the side)
(pick again)
(pick again)
(pick again)
(pick again)


; AutoLISP
(command "_OFFSET" 100.0 ent '(0 1000) "")
tools.notes: Offsetting a closed polyline inwards past its own radius collapses or removes segments - set OFFSETGAPTYPE and check the result. Circles and arcs offset to a different radius, not to a true parallel curve, which is what you want for a pipe but not always for a profile. The Erase and Layer settings are sticky and catch people out sessions later; the header line at the prompt always shows the current state.

tools.name: MIRROR
tools.description: Create a reflected copy of the selected objects about a mirror line defined by two points, optionally deleting the originals. It halves the work on symmetrical parts and layouts. Text, attributes and dimension text are kept readable by default so a mirrored drawing does not come out back to front.
tools.usage:
MIRROR  (alias MI)
Select objects: <selection>
Select objects: Enter
Specify first point of mirror line: <point>
Specify second point of mirror line: <point>
Erase source objects? [Yes/No] <N>: Y | N | Enter

parameters.name: mirror line
parameters.description: Two points defining the axis of reflection; use ORTHO or typed coordinates to keep it exactly horizontal or vertical.

parameters.name: Erase source objects
parameters.description: Yes turns the operation into a flip, No keeps both halves.

parameters.name: MIRRTEXT
parameters.description: System variable: 0 (the default) keeps text, attributes and mtext readable; 1 mirrors them as true geometry, which is what a stencil or a reversed print needs.

parameters.name: blocks and attributes
parameters.description: Block references are mirrored as a whole; their attribute text follows MIRRTEXT like any other text.

tools.example:
; Mirror a half-section about the vertical centre line, keeping both halves

ALL

0,0
0,100
N

; Flip a symbol left to right

MIRROR
L

50,0
50,100
Y

; AutoLISP

tools.notes: MIRRTEXT is a drawing variable saved with the file, so a drawing received from elsewhere may mirror text unexpectedly - check it before mirroring annotation. Mirroring with a negative scale in INSERT achieves the same flip for a single block reference. 3DMIRROR mirrors about a plane rather than a line.

tools.name: ARRAY
tools.description: Create multiple copies of objects in a regular pattern: rectangular rows and columns, polar copies around a centre, or items distributed along a path. It is the front end to ARRAYRECT, ARRAYPOLAR and ARRAYPATH, asking which type you want. Arrays are associative by default, meaning the whole pattern stays one object whose count, spacing and source geometry can be changed later with ARRAYEDIT.
tools.usage:
ARRAY  (alias AR)
Select objects: <selection>
Enter array type [Rectangular/PAth/POlar] <Rectangular>: R | PA | PO
(the prompts then continue as for ARRAYRECT, ARRAYPATH or ARRAYPOLAR)

; Legacy command-line version, non-associative
-ARRAY
Select objects: / Enter the type of array [Rectangular/POlar] <R>:

parameters.name: Rectangular / POlar / PAth
parameters.description: Which kind of array to build; the choice hands over to ARRAYRECT, ARRAYPOLAR or ARRAYPATH.

parameters.name: ARRAYTYPE
parameters.description: System variable holding the default array type offered by this command.

parameters.name: ASsociative
parameters.description: Yes keeps the pattern as a single associative array object; No produces independent copies, which is what older workflows and some downstream software expect.

parameters.name: ARRAYEDIT
parameters.description: The companion command that edits an existing associative array: Source to edit the original objects in place, REPlace to swap items, COUnt, Spacing, Rows, Levels, and RESet to restore erased items.

parameters.name: ARRAYCLOSE
parameters.description: Ends the in-place source editing state that ARRAYEDIT Source opens, saving or discarding the changes.

parameters.name: -ARRAY
parameters.description: The pre-2012 command-line version. It supports rectangular and polar only, is never associative, and needs no dialog - which is why scripts still use it.

tools.example:
; Associative rectangular array, 4 rows x 6 columns

L

R
COU
6
4
S
100
80

ALL

R
3
5
50

(select the array)
COU
8
4
tools.notes: EXPLODE on an array breaks the association permanently and leaves ordinary copies; ARRAYEDIT no longer applies afterwards. Editing one item of an associative array in place is done with ARRAYEDIT Source, ending with ARRAYCLOSE - editing the source updates every item. Use -ARRAY in scripts when a plain set of copies is wanted with no dialog and no associativity.

tools.name: ARRAYRECT
tools.description: Distribute copies of the selected objects into rows, columns and levels. After the initial grid appears, grips and command-line options adjust the counts and spacing live until you exit. It is the right tool for grids of columns, bolt patterns on a rectangular pitch, parking bays and tile layouts, and the resulting array stays editable.
tools.usage:
ARRAYRECT
Select objects: <selection>
Type = Rectangular  Associative = Yes
Select grip to edit array or
[ASsociative/Base point/COUnt/Spacing/COLumns/Rows/Levels/eXit] <eXit>:

parameters.name: COUnt (COU)
parameters.description: Number of columns and rows, asked in that order.

parameters.name: Spacing (S)
parameters.description: Distance between columns and between rows; negative values run the array left or down.

parameters.name: COLumns (COL)
parameters.description: Set the column count and spacing together, with a Total distance suboption that spreads the items over an overall length.

parameters.name: Rows (R)
parameters.description: Set the row count and spacing, plus an incremental elevation so each row steps up in Z.

parameters.name: Levels (L)
parameters.description: Number of levels and spacing in the Z direction, for 3D arrays.

parameters.name: ASsociative (AS)
parameters.description: Yes keeps one editable array object, No creates independent copies.

parameters.name: Base point (B)
parameters.description: The point of the array that is used for grip editing and as the reference for the spacing.

tools.example:
; M12 bolt pattern: 4 columns at 150, 3 rows at 200
ARRAYRECT
(select the hole)

COU
4
3
S
150
200
X

; Spread 10 columns evenly over a total of 9000
ARRAYRECT
L

COL
10
T
9000
X
tools.notes: Spacing is centre to centre, measured from the source object's base point, not edge to edge. ARRAYEDIT changes the counts and spacing later, and its Source option opens the original objects for editing so every item updates at once. Use a negative spacing rather than a negative count to run the pattern in the other direction.

tools.name: ARRAYPOLAR
tools.description: Copy objects evenly around a centre point. Give the centre, then the number of items and either the angle between them or the total angle to fill. It is the command for bolt circles, radial ribs, clock faces and stair treads around a newel, and whether the copies rotate with the pattern is controlled by the ROTate items option.
tools.usage:
ARRAYPOLAR
Select objects: <selection>
Specify center point of array or [Base point/Axis of rotation]: <point>
Type = Polar  Associative = Yes
Select grip to edit array or
[ASsociative/Base point/Items/Angle between/Fill angle/ROWs/Levels/ROTate items/eXit] <eXit>:

parameters.name: center point
parameters.description: The point the items are arrayed around; use an object snap to take it from existing geometry.

parameters.name: Items (I)
parameters.description: Number of items in the array, counting the source object.

parameters.name: Angle between (A)
parameters.description: Angle from one item to the next; positive is counter-clockwise under the default ANGDIR.

parameters.name: Fill angle (F)
parameters.description: Total angle the array spans; 360 for a full circle, a negative value to run clockwise.

parameters.name: ROTate items (ROT)
parameters.description: Yes rotates each copy so it faces the centre, No keeps every copy in its original orientation - the setting that decides whether arrayed text stays readable.

parameters.name: ROWs (ROW) / Levels (L)
parameters.description: Concentric rings of the same pattern, and copies stacked in Z.

parameters.name: Axis of rotation (A)
parameters.description: Two points defining a 3D axis to array about instead of a point in the current plane.

tools.example:
; Eight holes on a 200 PCD

8

100,0

L

With Fill angle 360 the angle between items is derived automatically; giving both Items and Angle between instead lets the array cover a partial arc. ROTate items No is almost always what annotation and block symbols need.

tools.name: ARRAYPATH
tools.description: Distribute copies of objects evenly along a path: a line, polyline, arc, circle, ellipse, spline or helix. The Method option chooses between Divide, which spreads a fixed number of items over the whole path, and Measure, which places items at a fixed spacing. Use it for fence posts, balusters, road furniture, chain links and sleepers on a curved alignment.
tools.usage:
ARRAYPATH
Select objects: <selection>
Select path curve: <curve>
Type = Path  Associative = Yes
Select grip to edit array or
[ASsociative/Method/Base point/Tangent direction/Items/Rows/Levels/Align items/Z direction/eXit] <eXit>:

parameters.name: Method (M)
parameters.description: Divide spreads a given number of items over the full path length; Measure places items at a given spacing and fills as much of the path as fits.

parameters.name: Items (I)
parameters.description: The item count, or with the Measure method the spacing between items.

parameters.name: Align items (A)
parameters.description: Yes rotates each copy to follow the path direction, No keeps them all parallel to the source.

parameters.name: Tangent direction (T)
parameters.description: Two points on the source object defining which way it points, so the alignment to the path is correct.

parameters.name: Base point (B)
parameters.description: The point of the source object that sits on the path.

parameters.name: Z direction (Z)
parameters.description: Whether the items keep the original Z direction or follow the 3D twist of the path.

parameters.name: Rows (R) / Levels (L)
parameters.description: Parallel rows offset from the path, and copies stacked in Z.

tools.example:
; Fence posts every 2000 along a polyline

(select the post block)

Changing the path later updates an associative path array automatically, which is why it is worth keeping the association. Align items combined with the right Tangent direction is what stops every second post facing backwards.

tools.name: ALIGN
tools.description: Move, rotate and optionally scale objects in one operation by giving pairs of source and destination points. One pair behaves like MOVE, two pairs move and rotate (and can scale to fit), and three pairs align objects in 3D. It is the fastest way to drop a detail onto a sloping surface or to fit a part between two known points.
tools.usage:
ALIGN  (alias AL)
Select objects: <selection>
Specify first source point: / Specify first destination point:
Specify second source point: / Specify second destination point:
Specify third source point or <continue>: Enter
Scale objects based on alignment points? [Yes/No] <N>: Y | N

parameters.name: one point pair
parameters.description: Behaves exactly like MOVE: the source point is placed on the destination point.

parameters.name: two point pairs
parameters.description: Moves and rotates the selection so the source points line up with the destination points in 2D.

parameters.name: three point pairs
parameters.description: Aligns objects in 3D, orienting them onto an arbitrary plane.

parameters.name: Scale objects
parameters.description: Yes uniformly scales the selection so the distance between the two source points becomes the distance between the two destination points - only offered with exactly two pairs.

tools.example:
; Drop a detail onto a sloping line and stretch it to fit
ALIGN
(select the detail)

0,0
(pick the lower end of the slope)
100,0
(pick the upper end of the slope)

Y

; AutoLISP form, no scaling
(command "_ALIGN" ss "" '(0 0) '(1000 500) '(100 0) '(1080 560) "" "_N")
tools.notes: Answering Yes to scaling distorts nothing because the scale is uniform, but it does change real dimensions - check the result before dimensioning. 3DALIGN is the newer command for 3D work and previews the result as you pick. When only rotation is needed, ROTATE with the Reference option is simpler.

tools.name: UNDO
tools.description: Reverse previous operations, with control over how they are grouped. The plain U command undoes one step; UNDO adds options to undo a number of steps, to place a Mark and roll back to it, and to wrap several commands in a BEgin/End group that later undoes as one. Scripts and macros use those grouping options so a long automated sequence can be reversed with a single undo.
tools.usage:
UNDO
Enter the number of operations to undo or
[Auto/Control/BEgin/End/Mark/Back] <1>: <n> | A | C | BE | E | M | B

U        ; undo one operation
UNDO C [All/None/One/Combine/Layer]

parameters.name: number
parameters.description: Undo that many operations in one step.

parameters.name: BEgin (BE) / End (E)
parameters.description: Open and close an undo group: everything between the two is treated as one operation. The standard wrapper around a script or LISP routine.

parameters.name: Mark (M) / Back (B)
parameters.description: Mark places a bookmark in the undo stream; Back rolls the drawing back to the most recent mark. With no mark set, Back offers to undo everything done in the session.

parameters.name: Control (C)
parameters.description: All enables full undo, None disables it and discards the undo file, One limits undo to a single command, Combine controls whether consecutive zooms and pans undo together, Layer whether layer dialog operations are combined.

parameters.name: Auto (A)
parameters.description: Controls whether all the actions of one menu item or macro are grouped as a single undo operation.

parameters.name: UNDOCTL / UNDOMARKS
parameters.description: Read-only system variables reporting the current undo state and the number of marks currently placed.

tools.example:
; Wrap a script so the whole thing undoes in one step
UNDO
BE
-LAYER
M
TEMP

CIRCLE
0,0
10
OFFSET
5
L
5,0

UNDO
E

; Later: reverse the entire block
U

; Mark a point and come back to it
UNDO
M
(experiment freely)
UNDO
B
tools.notes: UNDO Control None frees disk space on very large drawings but throws away all undo history, so it is rarely worth it. Some operations cannot be undone, including plotting, writing files and the commands that open or save a drawing. REDO immediately after an undo reverses it; MREDO reverses several.

tools.name: REDO
tools.description: Reverse the effect of the most recent UNDO or U. It must be issued immediately after the undo - any other command in between discards the redo information. MREDO is the multiple-step version, which can redo a given number of actions, all of them, or back to the last mark.
tools.usage:
REDO
(no prompts - reverses the last UNDO; Ctrl+Y)

MREDO
Enter number of actions or [All/Last]: <n> | A | L

parameters.name: immediacy
parameters.description: REDO only works directly after an undo. Once another command runs, the redo stack is gone.

parameters.name: MREDO number
parameters.description: Redo that many undone actions in one step.

parameters.name: MREDO All (A)
parameters.description: Redo everything that was undone.

parameters.name: MREDO Last (L)
parameters.description: Redo back to the last undo group or mark.

tools.example:
; Undo three steps, then change your mind
UNDO
3
MREDO
3

; Single step
U
REDO
tools.notes: The keyboard shortcuts are Ctrl+Z for undo and Ctrl+Y for redo. In scripts, avoid relying on redo at all: wrap the work in UNDO BEgin / UNDO End instead so the state is explicit. Closing and reopening a drawing clears both the undo and redo histories.

tools.name: PEDIT
tools.description: Edit 2D and 3D polylines: close or open them, join other objects onto them, set a uniform width, curve them with Fit or Spline, straighten them again with Decurve, reverse their direction and edit individual vertices. Selecting a line or arc offers to convert it to a polyline first, which is the usual way a drawing of loose lines becomes a set of closed, measurable outlines. The Multiple option processes many objects in one run.
tools.usage:
PEDIT  (alias PE)
Select polyline or [Multiple]: <object> | M
Object selected is not a polyline.  Do you want to turn it into one? <Y>
Enter an option [Close/Join/Width/Edit vertex/Fit/Spline/Decurve/Ltype gen/Reverse/Undo]:
(Edit vertex) [Next/Previous/Break/Insert/Move/Regen/Straighten/Tangent/Width/eXit]:

parameters.name: Join (J)
parameters.description: Add touching lines, arcs and polylines to the current polyline. With the Multiple option a fuzz distance can be given so small gaps are bridged.

parameters.name: Close (C) / Open (O)
parameters.description: Add or remove the closing segment. A truly closed polyline is required for reliable area calculation, hatching and extrusion.

parameters.name: Width (W)
parameters.description: Set one uniform width for every segment; the Edit vertex Width option sets a per-segment start and end width.

parameters.name: Fit (F)
parameters.description: Replace the straight segments with a smooth curve of arcs passing through every vertex.

parameters.name: Spline (S)
parameters.description: Pull the polyline into a spline-like curve controlled by the vertices; SPLINETYPE and SPLINESEGS decide the kind and smoothness.

parameters.name: Decurve (D)
parameters.description: Undo Fit or Spline and return to straight segments between the original vertices.

parameters.name: Ltype gen (L)
parameters.description: Generate the linetype pattern continuously along the whole polyline rather than restarting at each vertex; the PLINEGEN system variable sets the default for new polylines.

parameters.name: Multiple (M)
parameters.description: Select many objects at once; the chosen option is applied to all of them, which is how a whole drawing is converted and joined in one pass.

tools.example:
; Convert loose lines into closed polylines and join them
PEDIT
M
ALL

Y
J
0.5

C


; Give a polyline a 2 unit width and smooth it
PEDIT
(select the polyline)
W
2
F
X

SPLINEDIT is the equivalent for true spline objects, and the SPLINE command's Object option converts a spline-fitted polyline into a real spline. MLEDIT, the matching editor for multiline junctions such as crosses, tees and corner joints, is not given its own entry in this catalog.

tools.name: SPLINEDIT
tools.description: Edit a spline: move, add, delete or purge fit points, add and weight control vertices, raise the degree, change the start and end tangents, close or open the curve, reverse its direction, or convert it to a polyline. Use it to clean up an imported curve, to tighten a shape locally, or to hand a downstream system a polyline approximation instead of a NURBS curve.
tools.usage:
SPLINEDIT  (alias SPE)
Select spline: <object>
Enter an option [Close/Join/Fit data/Edit vertex/convert to Polyline/Reverse/Undo/eXit]:
(Fit data) [Add/Close/Delete/Kink/Move/Purge/Tangents/toLerance/eXit]:
(Edit vertex) [Add/Delete/Elevate order/Move/Weight/eXit]:

parameters.name: Fit data (F)
parameters.description: Work with the points the curve passes through: Add, Delete, Move, Kink (add a sharp point), Tangents, toLerance, and Purge which discards the fit data and leaves only control vertices.

parameters.name: Edit vertex (E)
parameters.description: Work with the control polygon: Add or Delete a vertex, Move one, change a vertex Weight so the curve is pulled harder towards it, or Elevate order to raise the degree and gain more vertices.

parameters.name: convert to Polyline (P)
parameters.description: Replace the spline with a polyline approximation to a given precision; PLINECONVERTMODE decides whether the result is made of line or arc segments.

parameters.name: Close (C) / Open (O)
parameters.description: Close the curve smoothly back on itself, or reopen a closed spline.

parameters.name: Join (J)
parameters.description: Join other splines, lines, arcs or polylines that meet the spline endpoint into one spline.

parameters.name: Reverse (R)
parameters.description: Flip the direction of the spline, which matters for path arrays, sweeps and text-bearing linetypes.

parameters.name: SPLFRAME
parameters.description: System variable that displays the control polygon so control-vertex editing can be seen.

tools.example:
; Purge the fit data and edit the control vertices instead

(select the spline)
F
P
E
W
(pick a vertex)
2.5
X
X

SPLINEDIT
(select the spline)
P
10
